analysis.one_liner: Requires drug companies to report deals that delay generic drugs to antitrust enforcers.
analysis.headline: The Drug Competition Act of 2000 never got a committee vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes pay generic drug makers to keep cheaper copies off the market, or cut other deals that slow generic competition. This bill would have forced both sides of any such deal to file it with the Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department within 10 business days, so federal antitrust enforcers could police agreements that limit the research, manufacture, or sale of generic drugs. Companies that failed to file could face fines of up to $20,000 per day and court orders forcing compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially seniors and families paying rising prescription drug prices, who would benefit from earlier generic competition and stronger antitrust oversight of brand-generic deals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers paying high prescription drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated findings note that prescription drug costs are rising at an alarming rate and are a major worry of senior citizens and American families, and that enhancing generic competition can significantly reduce those costs [S3].

It requires both the brand-name and generic manufacturer in any agreement that could limit the research, development, manufacture, marketing, or sale of a generic drug to file the agreement with the FTC and the Attorney General within 10 business days [S3].

The CRS summary describes the bill as requiring brand-name and generic drug manufacturers to file with the FTC and Attorney General any agreements that could limit the research, development, manufacture, marketing, or selling of a generic drug product [S2].
The bill gives enforcers teeth: civil fines of up to $20,000 per day of violation, plus court orders to force compliance and other equitable relief [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug manufacturers, which would bear new filing obligations, paperwork, legal costs, and exposure to per-day fines and antitrust scrutiny of their settlement deals.

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires notification; it does not itself ban deals that delay generics, so its effect depends entirely on whether FTC and Justice Department antitrust enforcement follows, which existing law already allows [S3].

It imposes new compliance costs on drug manufacturers of all sizes, including filing deadlines of 10 business days and civil penalties of up to $20,000 per day, with rulemaking authority for the FTC to demand additional documentary material [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that a transparency rule deters but does not prevent anticompetitive settlements; enforcement resources and courts still have to act on whatever the filings reveal [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is real but indirect: earlier warnings to antitrust enforcers about deals that keep cheap generics off the market, backed by meaningful per-day fines. The costs are modest compliance paperwork for drug companies. The main limitation is design, not cost: the bill adds visibility, not new legal standards, so its value hinges entirely on enforcers actually acting on what they receive.

outcome.mechanism: Leahy introduced it in July 2000 and the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the Drug Competition Act of 2000 on July 27, 2000, for himself and Sen. Herbert Kohl [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S1].
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill, and no vote ever occurred in the Senate before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers avoided new antitrust scrutiny of settlement deals that can delay cheaper generic competitors, and consumers kept paying the higher prices that follow such delays.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers; generic delays continued

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill took no further action on it; it never received a markup or a vote

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation to scrutinize brand-generic settlements and pay-for-delay deals, which threatened a common practice for extending brand-drug revenue

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only support on the record was its two Democratic sponsors, so the partisan shape of broader support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: Brand-name companies profit from keeping cheaper generic copies off the market, including through deals with generic makers, and the bill would force disclosure of such agreements to antitrust enforcers within 10 business days, with fines up to $20,000 per day for noncompliance. Its findings explicitly target brand-patent holders' private deals that restrain competition and raise drug costs [S3].

Generic firms that accept payments to delay their own products would face the same disclosure requirement and scrutiny, but generic makers as a class benefit from faster market entry once settlements can no longer quietly restrain competition [S3].

industries.industry: Federal antitrust enforcers (FTC and Justice Department)
industries.note: The bill hands the FTC and the Attorney General timely notice of every agreement affecting a generic's development or sale, making it easier to detect and challenge anticompetitive deals [S2].
